Thanks for the PR!

I originally used rich mainly for its support for multiple progress bars. I agree that the disk size of rich is extremely concerning for what's meant to be a lightweight modular library.

I will accept the PR, however, I think the progress bars are a nice addition for slower networks to see what's going on.
Do you think I should implement a lighter project like `tqdm`, or write a simple multi-progress bar loader that displays the download status of the files from each thread, or is having no progress bars at all a better solution?

`click.progressbar` can be used.
Example:
```python3
import click

content = "a" * 100_000

with click.progressbar(
    length=len(content),
    label='Downloading',
    show_percent=True,
    show_pos=True,
    width=50
) as bar:
    for char in content:
        bar.update(len(char))
```

I first changed from `rich` to `click.progressbar`.
But then I tested it and realized that it doesn't make sense - the files are very small and load almost instantly.
I suggest another way to reduce the size -- don't unzip the files after downloading, so that they are stored on disk as archives.

I added the commit so that zip-files don't unzip before saving. 
Reason:
fingerprint-network.zip = 756Kb
fingerprint-network.json = 11.8Mb
Would it be better if I use [msgspec](https://github.com/jcrist/msgspec) instead? It seems to benchmark faster than orjson, and supports much more platforms, including android arm64.

> But then I tested it and realized that it doesn't make sense - the files are very small and load almost instantly.

That makes sense. After thinking about it, a simple "Downloading model definition files" works fine as well.

Looks good!

msgspec makes sense to use if you need to validate data or get certain fields from json. But for that you need to write a data structure msgspec.Struct. 
In general, it doesn't make sense in our case, msgspec won't be faster than orjson.

There are some tests here, you can try to test the performance on downloaded json files:
https://gist.github.com/jcrist/80b84817e9c53a63222bd905aa607b43

Msgspec can also be used for dictionary encoding without `msg.Struct` with `msgspec.json.decode`. Here is my benchmark for reference:

```
Benchmarks:
- stdlib json: 0.60 ± 0.03
- orjson: 0.29 ± 0.03
- simdjson: 0.49 ± 0.03
- msgspec-dict: 0.27 ± 0.01  # Not using msg.Struct
- msgspec-struct: 0.21 ± 0.01  # Using msg.Struct
- pydantic-v2: 1.82 ± 0.51
```

BrowserForge's runtime speed relies pretty heavily on json encoding/decoding, so I worry that requiring users to install a specific extra like `pip install browserforge[orjson]` can add an extra layer of complexity for something so crucial.

Would you be open to considering an alternative to orjson?

`extract_json` is executed only once when the class is initialized.
In other functions that have `json.loads`, the execution time is very small and there is almost no difference.

That is, I don't think using even standard `json` will affect performance because json files are only loaded once when the class is initialized.

~If, of course, you initialize the class every time, the difference is noticeable. 
I mean, you shouldn't do that:~ The json files are class variables and are loaded once. So even if you do it this way, they are loaded only once.
```python3
from browserforge.fingerprints import FingerprintGenerator
for i in range(10):
    FingerprintGenerator().generate()
```

@daijro is it possible to inject generated fingerprint into hrequests or requests

> @daijro is it possible to inject generated fingerprint into hrequests or requests

Hi, BrowserForge headers can be easily set to a requests session (see [here](https://github.com/daijro/browserforge?tab=readme-ov-file#using-with-requests)).

Here are some examples:

## Using Requests

```py
import requests
from browserforge.headers import HeaderGenerator
# Create the header generator
headers = HeaderGenerator()
# Build the requests session
session = requests.Session()
session.headers = headers.generate()  # Set the session headers
# Send a request
resp = session.get('https://example.com')
print(resp.status_code)
```

If you're using Requests, you might also want to look into using [Hazetunnel](https://github.com/daijro/hazetunnel) to spoof the TLS fingerprint to match the User-Agent browser like hrequests does.

## Using Hrequests

```py
import hrequests
from browserforge.headers import HeaderGenerator
# Create a chrome header generator
headers = HeaderGenerator(browser='chrome')
# Build a chrome hrequests session
session = hrequests.Session(browser='chrome')
session.headers = headers.generate()  # Set the session headers
# Send a request
resp = session.get('https://example.com')
print(resp.status_code)
```

Note: Browserforge will be integrated into hrequests in an upcoming update.

Hello,

This feature was deprecated since it has become ineffective against nearly all modern anti-bots providers.

Browserforge uses Apify's fingerprint injector logic, which injects Javascript into the page to spoof browser data.

However, most WAFs are capable of identifying this. For instance, this line of code can easily detect nearly all libraries that spoof data by injecting JS:

```js
if( Object.getOwnPropertyNames(navigator)[0] ) alert('fake parameters detected');
```
Here's an article on why JS injection should not be used:
https://cpa.rip/stati/antidetect-palivo/

---

Camoufox is the successor to Browserforge's fingerprint injector. It intercepts data in the browser at the C++ level, making data injection undetectable through JS inspection.

Thanks a lot! I'd like to add some information about this bug because if you encounter it, in the next step you will very likely encounter what I did.

PyInstaller does not include data files from site-packages by default - it only includes Python modules.
If a library stores files in a separate folder (e.g., .yml, .json, .dat, templates, locale, etc.), these files will not be included in the exe, and the errors will recur.

Solution is quite simple: just go through each library in site-packages and add all its files to datas. Add the following lines in your .spec file:
```
from pathlib import Path
import sys

venv_site_packages = Path(sys.prefix) / "lib" / f"python{sys.version_info.major}.{sys.version_info.minor}" / "site-packages"

extra_datas = []

for pkg_dir in venv_site_packages.iterdir():
    if pkg_dir.is_dir() and not pkg_dir.name.startswith("__pycache__"):
        extra_datas.append((str(pkg_dir), pkg_dir.name))

a = Analysis(
    ...
    datas=extra_datas,
)
```
